They are never written straight into the GT sidecars (LAB-002, README section 1). /ball_check shows them, uncertain first: Claude and the detector disagree, low confidence, cell corrections. A "yes" writes the box with a human_checked marker (tier 2). A drag or a tap-to-place writes labeller (tier 1). This closes the documented gap that a ball verdict is thrown away; see section 9.
  8. Ingest, re-score, propose. Verdicts go through the existing ingest, the tracker is re-scored with the ball tracking eval, and a retrain is proposed (never started automatically) when enough new tier 1 or tier 2 labels exist. "Enough" is not decided; see open questions.

docs.title: 3. One clip, in order
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
  participant J as Loop job
  participant D as Detector and tracker
  participant C as Crop tool
  participant L as Claude backend
  participant P as Candidate pool
  participant H as Person in ball_check
  participant S as Sidecar and store
  J->>J: refuse if clip is held out
  J->>L: overview, 3 small frames per window
  L-->>J: scene state per second, coarse region
  J->>D: candidates and one path per frame
  D-->>J: boxes, conf, tracker path
  J->>C: frames with no candidate near the path
  C->>D: upscaled crop, detect again
  D-->>J: extra candidates
  J->>L: zoomed crop, numbered boxes, grid
  L-->>J: verdict, chosen number or cell, confidence, reason
  J->>P: proposals, tier 3, with model and prompt version
  P->>H: uncertain first
  H->>S: yes writes human_checked, drag or tap writes labeller
  S->>J: verdicts ingested, re-score

The sequence shows that the person only ever sees what Claude and the detector have already narrowed down, and that nothing reaches the sidecars without a person's action.

docs.title: 4. Prompt and answer format
docs.text:
Claude is given multiple choice, never a request for pixel coordinates. A language model is unreliable at locating an 11 px object by number of pixels, so the question is shaped so that a position is always chosen from a list the code drew.

Verify prompt (one per frame, planned):

  • Input: a padded, zoomed crop around the expected ball position (at least 6 box sides of padding, the same default that /ball_check uses, LAB-1008), with candidate boxes drawn and numbered 1..n, plus, on a separate copy, a fine numbered grid over the crop (for example 6 by 6, cells 1..36; the grid size is proposed and to be tuned).
  • Question: "Which numbered box is the match ball, or none? If none, but you can see the ball, which grid cell is it in?"
  • Context given in words: ball in play versus replay, football size and colour, that boot and head blobs and ad-board marks are common false positives.

Answer (strict JSON, planned):

{
  "verdict": "box | cell | none_visible | not_sure",
  "box": 2,
  "cell": null,
  "confidence": 0.0,
  "reason": "one short sentence"
}

Rules:

  • verdict is box (the ball is one of the numbered boxes), cell (the ball is visible but no box is on it), none_visible, or not_sure.
  • confidence is a number from 0 to 1. It is Claude's own and is not calibrated; the calibration run (section 8) measures how far to trust it.
  • cell is a correction hint. A cell alone is never a box: a person places the ball, or the crop-and-re-detect step runs again inside that cell.
  • A malformed or off-list answer is recorded as not_sure. It is never repaired by guessing.

Logged with every answer: clip, frame, crop geometry, the candidate list as drawn, the raw answer, the model name, the prompt version, the backend and its settings, the time taken, and the cost where the backend reports one. This log is the data the calibration run and any later audit depend on.

docs.title: 5. Backends
docs.text:
The Claude call sits behind one small interface (planned): a request (images, candidate list, prompt version) goes in, a structured answer comes out. Two backends, selectable by configuration:

(a) Anthropic API (b) Claude Code headless (claude -p) Sign-in API key Subscription login Cost model Pay per token; cost is reported per call Counts against the plan's usage limits, shared with interactive use, so a loop can starve the person's own sessions Speed and control Parallel calls, fixed model and settings, structured output, retries are yours to control Slower, one process per call, less control over settings and output shape Fit An unattended, continuous loop Personal use, small batches, the calibration run if no key is available

Recommendation: use the API for an unattended continuous loop, and keep claude -p as a fallback for small or interactive runs. Check the current terms of the subscription before relying on headless use for anything beyond personal work. The pluggable interface means the choice can change without touching the loop.

Handling the key: it lives in the job runner's secret store or the environment of the job. It never goes in the repo, a config file in git, a log line, or this site.

docs.title: Running it: jobs, not a service
docs.text:
The loop is a sequence of jobs under an external job runner (Prefect: a server on a small always-on machine, with a work pool on the GPU machine). That setup is not in this repo, and the design does not depend on it: every step must also run as a plain script that takes a clip list and an output folder, writes only under that folder, and can be re-run safely. Planned jobs, in order:

  1. pick unlabelled clips, new matches first (reads the held-out registry);
  2. detector and tracker (GPU);
  3. crop and re-detect (GPU);
  4. Claude verify (network, no GPU);
  5. queue for review (write the candidate pool);
  6. ingest verdicts (ingest_gt, which already reads Ball Check verdicts);
  7. re-score with the ball tracking eval (CPU, about 7 s for 26 clips and three trackers per Ball tracking evaluation);
  8. propose a retrain when enough new tier 1 or 2 labels exist (a notification, not a training run).

docs.title: 6. Provenance and tiers
docs.text:
Tiers as in Datasets and labels; the new rows are planned.

What Sidecar tags Tier Written by Counts as ground truth in the ball eval? Reaches training? Hand-drawn or dragged box [label, labeller] 1 A person Yes, the headline human tier Yes Propagated box a person checked [label, vittrack, human_checked] 2 Machine, then a person Separate human+propagated tier only Yes Claude proposal a person said yes to (planned) [label, claude, human_checked] 2 Claude, then a person No; unknown provenance is ignored (detection_replay.py:214-219), and should stay so Yes Claude proposal after a drag or a tap to place (planned) [label, labeller] 1 A person, using Claude's hint Yes Yes Claude proposal, not yet reviewed (planned) none: it lives only in the candidate pool 3 Claude No No Detector box (route F) [label, rtdetr] in machine_labels/ 3 Machine No Only via Ball Check

Rules:

  • A Claude proposal is never written straight into a sidecar. This is LAB-002 ("machine output never replaces anything at or above its own level", README section 1). Nothing at tier 1 or 2 is ever overwritten by it.
  • A "yes" in /ball_check writes the box with human_checked. A drag, or a tap on the spot where the ball is, writes labeller. Both are the person's act, not Claude's.
  • Tier 2 for a Claude box keeps the claude tag, so a later audit can tell which labels came through the loop. The ingest map from provenance tag to source (ingest_gt.py:82-87) and the session's provenance set would need a claude entry; until then an unknown tag is handled by the fallbacks listed in Architecture, section 6 and must not be relied on.

docs.title: 7. The held-out rule
docs.text:
Held-out clips never enter the loop. They stay human-only.

  • The held-out set is the 6 clips (119 human ball frames, 7 no-ball frames) in Ball tracking evaluation, plus whatever is added later. A clip is held out if it, or its source footage, is outside the detector's training data.
  • The loop reads a checked-in held-out registry (planned; it relates to T-33, the explicit eval-clip list) and refuses any clip in it, matched by canonical clip id (footy_track.clip_id) and by footage time span, since names alone cannot catch overlap (T-33).
  • Claude output never enters a held-out clip's sidecar, the candidate pool for it, or the training export for it.
  • New held-out clips are added from new matches over time, human-marked, before the loop first touches that match. One full match is held out per match batch, as Best pipeline step 4 already says.
  • Why it matters: a detector retrained on Claude-assisted labels of a clip, then scored on that clip, measures nothing. The rule keeps the score honest.

docs.title: 8. Calibration plan and acceptance thresholds
docs.text:
Calibrate before scaling. The thresholds below are proposed, not agreed.

Data. The 26 clips with human marks: 646 human ball frames and 37 human no-ball frames (Ball tracking evaluation). Steps 3 to 6 of the loop (candidates, crop and re-detect, Claude verify) run over them read-only. Output goes to a scratch folder, never to the candidate pool or a sidecar, because 6 of the 26 clips are held out and the loop must not write into them. For the same reason, tune the prompt on the 20 seen clips only and score the 6 held-out clips once, at the end. The eval's own caveats carry over: the marks are mostly on frames a person looked at because the detector proposed something, so recall will look better than it is.

Extra negatives: the 37 no-ball frames are few. Add the not_ball Ball Check verdicts (144 in Best pipeline, section 3, stored in detection_review) as false-positive examples.

What to measure, and a proposed threshold for each:

Measure Definition Proposed threshold Why Agreement with human marks Of human-marked ball frames where a correct candidate exists, the share where Claude picks it at least 0.95 Below that, the review queue fills with disagreements and saves little False "not ball" Claude says none_visible or picks another box when the human mark is among the candidates at most 0.03 These are real balls the loop would discard False "ball" Claude confirms a box on a no-ball frame, or one more than 25 px from a human mark, or a box a person marked not_ball at most 0.02 A confirmed wrong box becomes an anchor and misleads the fill. Held-out WRONG is the failure the tracker eval already watches Beats the confidence bands Claude's precision on candidates of conf 0.1 to 0.6, where measured precision is at most 0.42 (Best pipeline, Ball Check precision) clearly above 0.42 in every band Otherwise Claude adds nothing the confidence score did not give Extra balls from crop and re-detect Human-marked frames with no original candidate within 25 px where the re-detect finds one within 25 px report the count; proceed if it recovers a useful share of the 112 frames the detector missed (646 frames, minus 534 with a candidate within 25 px: 74 held-out plus 460 seen, from Ball tracking evaluation) This is the step meant to raise recall; if it finds nothing, the loop is only a faster reviewer Calibration of Claude's confidence Precision per Claude-confidence band monotone and usable to order the review queue Needed for "uncertain first" Cost and time per clip Backend cost and wall time per clip, split by step set after the first run, against a budget stated before it; compare per resolved frame with the human 3.3 s per card (Best pipeline, route D) No cost number exists yet (unverified)

Gate. The loop is not run on new matches until agreement, false "not ball" and false "ball" meet their thresholds on the seen clips and the single held-out scoring does not contradict them. If the thresholds are missed, the fallback is a smaller role (for example the overview pass and crop-and-re-detect only, with a person doing every verify), not lower thresholds.

docs.title: Calibration results (pilot, 2026-11)
docs.text:
A first calibration pilot has been run. It is small, uses the subscription backend, and does not clear the gate: on every proposed threshold the first prompt version misses. Treat the numbers as a baseline for iterating the prompt and the crop step, not as a verdict on the idea.

Method. Code: src/footy_track/autolabel/ and scripts/claude_verify_pilot.py (prepare, ask, score; tests in tests/test_autolabel_verify_pilot.py, synthetic data only). Steps, in order:

  1. Frames. All human-marked frames of the 6 held-out clips (119 ball, 7 no-ball) plus a seeded sample of the seen clips: 50 ball frames where a cached detector candidate lies within 25 px of the human mark, 50 where none does, and 20 no-ball frames. 246 questions in a fixed shuffled order. Only labeller (human-placed) marks count as GT. The GT is used only to stratify the sample and to score; it never places a crop or a candidate.
  2. Crop centre. The bidirectional tracker's output replayed over the cached detections (172 frames), else the nearest tracker position within 12 frames (59), else the frame centre (15). The crop is 320 x 320 native pixels, clamped to the frame.
  3. Crop and re-detect. The crop is upscaled 3x (960 x 960) and the same RT-DETR weights run on it at conf 0.05 and imgsz 960 (the 3x scale with no further resampling; other scales are unmeasured). Candidates are the cached boxes inside the crop plus the re-detect boxes, de-duplicated within 6 px (the original wins), top 6 by confidence; each remembers where it came from.
  4. Question image. The crop shown at 960 x 960 with thin coloured boxes, a large number beside each box, a faint 8 x 8 grid labelled A1 to H8 at the edges (one cell is 40 px at native resolution), and a 480 x 270 whole-frame thumbnail with the crop outlined. The list of numbers with detector confidences is drawn beside it.
  5. Ask. claude -p (Claude Code headless, subscription login), one call per 6 images, each image read with the Read tool, reply a JSON array. Answer schema: {"verdict": "candidate" | "cell" | "none" | "unsure", "candidate": int | null, "cell": "C5" | null, "confidence": 0 to 1, "reason": short}. This differs from the sketch in section 4 (8 x 8 grid instead of 6 x 6, candidate/none/unsure as verdict names). The exact prompt text is versioned in claude_cli.py as verify-v1. A malformed batch is retried once. Sonnet on all 246 questions; Opus on the first 60 (a random subset, by the shuffle).
  6. Score. Per question against the human marks within R = 25 px (and 10 px) at native resolution. Ball present: correct if the chosen candidate's centre, or the chosen cell's centre, is within R of the mark; none is a false "not ball"; unsure is counted separately. No-ball: correct only for none; any candidate or cell is a false "ball". A wrong pick on a ball frame also counts as a false "ball".

Prompt tuning. None. verify-v1 was run once, unchanged, on seen and held-out frames together, so the held-out numbers are not contaminated by tuning, and there is no tuned-on-seen result either.

Results, Sonnet, R = 25 px (at 10 px every rate moves by at most 0.03 and the headline conclusions do not change):

set questions agreement agreement where a candidate is within R false "not ball" (all ball frames) false "not ball" (candidate within R) false "ball" (all questions) unsure all 246 0.512 0.771 (101 of 131) 0.397 0.153 0.102 0.033 held-out 126 0.516 0.833 (60 of 72) 0.395 0.125 0.095 0.016 seen 120 0.508 0.695 (41 of 59) 0.400 0.186 0.108 0.050

Other rows: false "ball" on the 27 no-ball frames alone is 0.185 (5 of 27; held-out 2 of 7, seen 3 of 20). Wrong picks on ball frames are 0.091 of ball frames. No malformed answers, no retries for Sonnet.

The crop often misses the ball. In 57 of the 219 ball questions (26%; 28 of 119 held-out) the human mark is outside the 320 px crop, because the tracker's expected position was wrong or absent. There the only right answer for the crop is none, which the strict scoring above counts as a false "not ball". Two extra views: counting none as correct when the mark is outside the crop, agreement is 0.699 (held-out 0.698); and on the 162 ball questions whose mark is inside the crop, agreement is 0.642 and the false "not ball" rate is 0.253. The crop step, not only Claude, limits the pilot.

Cell answers. 12 questions got a cell answer from Sonnet; 3 were within 25 px (a 40 px cell centre is up to about 28 px from a ball in the same cell, so 25 px is a lenient test for a cell). On the 88 ball frames with no candidate within R in the crop, agreement was 0.034, so the cell hint is not a usable way to recover a ball the detector misses.

Crop-and-re-detect gain. Of the 219 ball questions, 14 (6.4%; 5 of 119 held-out, 9 of 100 seen) had a candidate within 25 px only because of the re-detect pass (the cached run had none inside the crop). Of the 102 ball frames with no cached candidate within 25 px in the crop, that is 14%. Sonnet picked the right box on 4 of those 14 (2 of 5 held-out); Opus picked it on 1 of the 3 that fall in its 60-question subset. So the step does add balls, but few, and Claude does not yet pick most of them.

Sonnet versus Opus, on the same 60 questions (53 ball frames, 7 no-ball; 30 held-out, 30 seen), R = 25 px:

model agreement agreement where a candidate is within R false "not ball" (candidate within R) false "not ball" (mark in crop) false "ball" unsure Sonnet 0.567 0.778 (28 of 36) 0.139 0.233 0.100 0.033 Opus 0.600 0.861 (31 of 36) 0.028 (1 of 36) 0.093 0.117 0.117

Opus is far less likely to throw away a real ball, and says unsure more often (0.117 against 0.033); it is no better on false "ball". With 60 questions, one or two answers move any of these by 0.02 to 0.03, so the difference is indicative only.

Confidence calibration (R = 25 px, share of answers in each band that were correct): Sonnet 0.23 (7 of 31) below 0.5, 0.32 (26 of 81) from 0.5 to 0.8, 0.69 (93 of 134) from 0.8; Opus 0 of 11, 8 of 18, 28 of 31 (0.90). Both are monotone, so the confidence can order a review queue, but even the top band is below the 0.95 target for Sonnet. The comparison with the detector's confidence bands (precision at most 0.42) was not run.

Against the proposed thresholds (all on Sonnet and all frames unless stated; none met):

measure proposed pilot met agreement at least 0.95 0.512 strict, 0.699 mark-in-crop adjusted, 0.771 where a candidate exists (held-out 0.833) no false "not ball" at most 0.03 0.153 where a candidate exists (Opus 0.028 on 36 frames); 0.397 on all ball frames Sonnet no; Opus only in that narrow slice false "ball" at most 0.02 0.102 (Sonnet), 0.117 (Opus, 60 questions) no

Time and cost. Sonnet: 41 calls (6 images each), mean 23.6 s, reported cost USD 0.091 per call (3.73 in total). Opus: 11 calls (one malformed batch was retried once and then parsed), mean 32.0 s, USD 0.171 per call (1.88 in total). The reported cost is the list-price equivalent printed by the CLI; on the subscription it is a usage figure, not a charge. Each call also carries about 7,000 tokens of the CLI's own context. Projection for a 30 s clip at 2 frames per second (60 questions, 10 calls): Sonnet about 4 minutes of calls run one after another (about 80 s at 3 in parallel) and about USD 0.91; Opus about 5.3 minutes (about 110 s at 3 in parallel) and about USD 1.71. That is roughly 4 s (Sonnet) or 5 s (Opus) per question, against 3.3 s per card for a person, before any human review of what Claude flags. The GPU steps (reading frames, re-detect on 246 crops, drawing) took under a minute on a single consumer GPU and are not split out.

Caveats.

  • 6 held-out clips and 126 held-out questions: every rate has a wide interval (for example 28 of 36 has a 95% interval of roughly 0.60 to 0.90). The Opus comparison is 60 questions.
  • The subscription backend shares usage limits with interactive work and was not tuned (no temperature or settings control); results may differ on the API.
  • The seen sample is stratified by whether a detector candidate exists, so the overall rates are not the rates on a typical clip. The human marks are mostly frames a person looked at because the detector proposed something (section 8); the eval's caveats carry over.
  • Some of the human marks are themselves hard to confirm at this scale (a ball in a crowd, a ball behind an advert board). Claude's "none" on those frames is not clearly an error. The pilot has no second human pass to check the marks.
  • A contact sheet of wrong answers and re-detect wins was inspected only to sanity check the rendering; the prompt was not changed in response.
  • Crop scale (3x), imgsz 960 for re-detect, 8 x 8 grid and 6 boxes per question are untuned choices.

What it suggests, not proves. Fixing the crop first (the mark is outside it in a quarter of the frames) and re-running before touching the prompt; trying Opus or a second look on none answers where a candidate exists; and not relying on cell answers. The gate in this section stays: no new matches until the thresholds are met.

docs.title: Method v2 results (2026-11)
docs.text:
The reviewer's fixes to the pilot were built and scored. The gate is still not met. v2 is much better than v1 on the held-out clips, but agreement, false "not ball" and false "ball" all miss their thresholds, and 35% of the human-marked ball frames cannot be answered at all because the detector and the re-detect pass produce no candidate near the mark.

What changed from v1. Code: autolabel/verify_v2.py, render_v2.py, prompts_v2.py, scripts/claude_verify_v2.py (prepare, ask, score; tests in tests/test_autolabel_verify_v2.py, synthetic data only).

  1. Crops are centred on each candidate, not on the tracker's expected position, so the mark can no longer fall outside the crop for lack of a tracker guess.
  2. One question per candidate: "is the box on the match ball?", strict JSON {"verdict": "ball" | "not_ball" | "unsure", "confidence": 0 to 1, "reason": short}. The image is a 128 px native patch enlarged 4x to 512 px with a single thin yellow box, plus a 384 px context panel at 1x with the patch outlined. No grid cells. This is the question /ball_check asks a person.
  3. Candidates per frame: the detection the bidirectional tracker chose (if any; source tracker), the top 2 other cached candidates by confidence (top), and up to 2 crop-and-re-detect candidates (redetect: a 320 px crop around the tracker path, 3x upscale, same weights, conf 0.05) that have no cached candidate within 25 px. Every question records its source.
  4. Models: Opus by default; optional "Sonnet first, Opus second look on not_ball and unsure" (ask --only-from). The claude -p backend strips API-key variables from the environment and stops with a distinct exit code on an auth or usage-limit error; there is no fallback backend (the API backend is not wired).
  5. Scoring: per candidate, a candidate within R = 25 px of a human mark is "near", any other is "far". A ball frame is correct when exactly the near candidates are answered ball and no far one is; a no-ball frame when none is. Reported: precision and recall of ball verdicts, frame agreement, false "not ball" (near candidates answered not_ball), false "ball" (far candidates, including those on no-ball frames, answered ball), unsure rate, the split by source and by Claude confidence, and held-out against seen. Ball frames with no candidate within R are reported apart and are not counted against Claude; their far candidates still count toward false "ball".
  6. Protocol: the prompt was iterated on seen clips only, three versions, then the held-out clips were scored once with the last one. Sample as v1 (same seed): all 126 held-out frames, and for tuning the first 80 frames of the seeded seen sample (279 questions; 39 ball frames answerable, 27 with no candidate within R, 13 no-ball frames).

Prompt versions (exact text in prompts_v2.py; a logged prompt_version always maps to its text):

version change verify-v2 plain question, list of look-alikes, unsure allowed verify-v2.1 after reading v2's errors: the ball may be yellow, yellow-green or lilac (hi-vis balls were called boots and socks); say ball when the ball is in, touching, or within about one box height of the box (many "false not ball" were a box 10 to 25 px off a clearly visible ball) verify-v2.2 v2.1 plus a strict look-alike rule (a ball is a separate round object, not part of a boot, sock, board or crowd; a faint smear is unsure) after v2.1 raised false "ball"

Seen clips (tuning set), Opus, R = 25 px (46 near and 233 far candidates):

prompt frame agreement (39 frames) no-ball frames (13) ball precision ball recall false "not ball" false "ball" (far) unsure v2 0.590 0.846 0.689 0.674 0.239 0.060 0.097 v2.1 0.564 0.692 0.578 0.804 0.174 0.116 0.047 v2.2 0.538 0.769 0.642 0.739 0.174 0.082 0.104 v2.2, Sonnet 0.538 0.769 0.732 0.652 0.196 0.047 0.140

The three prompts are within noise of each other on 39 frames (one frame is 0.026). v2.2 was chosen as final before the held-out run because it had the lowest sum of false "not ball" and false "ball". Sonnet with the final prompt is close to Opus, says unsure more, and costs half as much per question; a Sonnet-first design saves little here because 85% of its answers (not_ball or unsure) would need an Opus second look.

Held-out clips, scored once, verify-v2.2, Opus, R = 25 px (126 frames: 119 ball, 7 no-ball; 355 questions: 83 tracker, 167 top, 105 redetect; 76 near and 279 far candidates):

measure result threshold met frame agreement, ball frames with a candidate within R 0.813 (61 of 75) at least 0.95 no false "not ball" (near candidates not answered ball) 0.079 (6 of 76; 1 of them unsure) at most 0.03 no false "ball" (far candidates answered ball) 0.108 (30 of 279; no-ball frames alone 0.087, 2 of 23; 17 are on ball frames with no near candidate) at most 0.02 no ball precision / recall 0.697 (69 of 99) / 0.908 (69 of 76) no-ball frame agreement 0.714 (5 of 7) unsure rate 0.070 ball frames with no candidate within R (not answerable) 44 of 119 (0.370); only 2 of them had a cached candidate within R that was not selected

At R = 10 px the rates move by 0.01 to 0.02. Where the answers are good: the candidate the tracker chose is confirmed with precision 0.952 (59 of 62), the other top candidates only 0.242 (8 of 33), re-detect 0.5 (2 of 4). Claude's confidence orders the answers well: ball verdicts with confidence at least 0.95 were all near a mark (33 of 33), 0.8 to 0.95 gave 28 of 43, 0.5 to 0.8 gave 8 of 23. The detector's own confidence bands on the same candidates were 16 of 223 near below 0.3, 7 of 65 from 0.3 to 0.6 and 53 of 67 from 0.6 to 0.9, so Claude is clearly above the detector's low-confidence precision (at most 0.42), mainly by rejecting the many far candidates.

Crop-and-re-detect. Three held-out ball frames had a near candidate only from the re-detect pass (the cached run had none within 25 px); Claude confirmed 2 of them. Against 44 unanswerable frames this is a small gain; the frames that remain unanswerable are real misses of both the detector and the re-detect pass, so the method cannot raise recall on them.

Cost and time. Opus, held-out run: 46 calls (45 batches of 8 images and one retry), mean 44 s per call, 5.6 s per question one after another (about 11 minutes with 3 in parallel), list-price-equivalent USD 0.0127 per question (4.61 in total). Sonnet on the seen set: USD 0.0058 per question, 2.8 s per question. A frame has about 2.8 questions, so about 16 s and USD 0.036 per frame with Opus, against 3.3 s per card for a person. On a subscription the cost is a usage figure, not a charge.

Reading the result.

  • Most remaining errors are of three kinds. (a) False "ball" on far candidates: a second ball-like blob in the same frame (a spare ball, a bright patch near an advert board) that Claude cannot distinguish from the match ball in isolation; a per-candidate question has no way to know that only one is the match ball. (b) False "not ball" on near candidates where the human mark is a blurred or partly hidden ball, or a ball inside the crowd, where Claude's not_ball is arguably right; the marks have no second human pass. (c) The 10 to 25 px offsets, which v2.1 and v2.2 only partly fixed.
  • The 0.95 agreement target looks out of reach for per-candidate verdicts alone. A frame-level step (accept a ball only when it agrees with the tracker's chosen detection, take the highest-confidence ball when several are returned, and send everything else to a person) would use the observed structure: ball verdicts at confidence at least 0.95 were all correct. That combination was not scored here and is not tuned on seen clips; treat it as the next experiment, not as a result.
  • Caveats: held-out is 6 clips and 126 frames, so every rate has a wide interval (61 of 75 has a 95% interval of roughly 0.71 to 0.89); the seen tuning set is a stratified sample with half of its ball frames unanswerable, so its rates are not comparable with held-out rates; prompt versions differ by one or two frames; the marks are mostly frames a person looked at because the detector proposed something.

docs.title: Re-checking the disagreements
docs.text:
The held-out marks have no second human pass, and the 36 disagreements (7 false "not ball" including one unsure, 30 false "ball") include many that look like mark problems: a clear ball at a player's feet while the mark sits elsewhere, a spare ball near the hoardings, a mark on a ball in the crowd, a mark on a blurred smudge. A person re-checks each one, and the metrics are then re-computed against the marks as corrected. No new schema:

  1. claude_verify_v2 disagreements --run R --answers A --videos V lists every disagreement (disagreements.csv and .json: clip, frame, mark position, Claude's box, confidence, type) and writes review_list.json, one Ball Check card per human mark ("is the mark the in-play match ball?") and one per disagreeing Claude box (same question), grouped by frame, mark first. A card shows its own box; the other box of the pair is drawn in magenta, so one card shows both.
  2. Start the labeller with FOOTY_BALL_CHECK_LIST=R/review_list.json (and FOOTY_CLIPS_DIR set to the folder the videos are in) and open /ball_check?source=list. This is the smallest piece of T-47's pool: explicit cards served in file order, no sampling. It is not the claude candidate pool (tier 3, human_checked write) that T-47 plans.
  3. Verdicts go to the normal log (<gt dir>/ball_checks/<clip>.jsonl, source: "list"), so the feature store import sees them like any others. They are left out of the /ball_check/stats precision and of the confidence bands (the cards are hand-picked, not a sample).
  4. score ... --decisions <gt dir>/ball_checks re-scores with the marks changed by those verdicts and writes summary_<label>_rechecked.json and truth_<label>_rechecked.json.

Mapping of answers (nothing new is added): on a mark card, not_ball removes the mark, corrected (drag the box) moves it, ball, box_off, unsure or no answer keep it. On a Claude card, ball adds that box as a mark, corrected adds the dragged box, not_ball, unsure or no answer add nothing. So "GT right" is mark ball plus Claude not_ball; "Claude right" is mark not_ball plus Claude ball; "both wrong" is both not_ball (the frame becomes a no-ball frame); and a spare or crowd ball is not_ball for the question asked (the in-play ball). That last case cannot be told apart from "not a ball at all" in the log; if the split matters later, a distinct verdict (for example not_in_play) would be a schema change and is proposed here, not made.

Limits: the list holds only disagreements, so it cannot find a wrong mark on a frame where Claude and the mark agree, or on the 44 frames with no candidate near the mark. A dragged corrected box is appended to the sidecar as new labeller GT (the existing save_box behaviour) and does not delete the old mark, so a corrected mark leaves two lines for the frame until the old one is removed. The mark cards use a 12 px square because the run stores mark centres only.

docs.title: 9. What the code does with verdicts today
docs.text:
This corrects a claim older pages still make. T-02 is merged: Ball Check verdicts reach the feature store.

  • ingest_gt imports the verdict logs: import_ball_checks(store, bc_dir, ...) (feature_store/ingest_gt.py:383) into the detection_review table (feature_store/schema.py:330).
  • The training export drops boxes a person marked not_ball unless asked to keep them (scripts/export_training_dataset.py:85-97, applied at :125 and :151).
  • Still open: the import matches by box overlap but stores the positional detection_id, and the export joins on it (T-25); ball verdicts mark a detection reviewed, but nothing yet creates a tier 2 box from a yes.
  • No code creates human_checked. Since T-01 the labeller session keeps the marker across load and flush (labeller/session.py:173-180, :326-332), and ingest_gt reads it (ingest_gt.py:81). A "yes writes human_checked" step is therefore new work (T-47).

docs.title: 10. Risks
docs.text: Risk What it looks like Mitigation (proposed) Claude agrees with a detector false positive A player's head near the ad boards at conf about 0.75 is already followed by a tracker (T-34); numbered boxes invite the model to pick one Always offer "none"; include hard cases in calibration; ask a person whenever Claude and the detector or tracker path disagree; never treat a Claude yes as tier 2 without a person Leakage Claude-assisted labels of an eval clip reach training, or the prompt is tuned on held-out clips The held-out rule (section 7); tune on seen clips only; registry checked in code, not by convention Cost Per-frame calls over thousands of frames per match Verify only frames the tracker cannot settle; crop sizes small; measure cost in calibration; a budget cap per run; API cost is reported per call Wrong anchors poison the fill One confirmed wrong box drags the bidirectional fill Anchors need agreement between Claude and a candidate from detector or re-detect; the tracker's own agreement test applies Optimistic calibration The 26 clips are frames people already looked at Say so in the result; treat thresholds as necessary, not sufficient; re-measure on the first reviewed batch from a new match Model or prompt drift The same prompt gives different answers after a model change Log model and prompt version on every answer; re-run a fixed calibration subset when either changes Subscription limits (backend b) The loop uses up the plan for interactive work Use the API for the loop Overview pass misleads Scene state is wrong, a real play is skipped It only suggests where to look and what to skip; it never gives positions or labels Human fatigue and rubber-stamping A person taps yes on every Claude proposal Mix in known-answer cards; keep the uncertain-first order; sample-check reviewed batches Public repo Keys, hosts or paths leak into docs or logs Secrets only in the runner; logs hold no keys

docs.title: 11. Open questions
docs.text:
1. How many new tier 1 and 2 labels justify proposing a retrain? One match's worth, or a fixed count?
  2. Should a claude plus human_checked box count as tier 2 in the training export, or be exported only after a second look? It is not independent evidence, so the ball eval ignores it.
  3. Grid size for cell answers: coarse (fewer, larger cells) or fine (more cells, harder to read)? Tune in calibration.
  4. Is the overview pass worth its cost? Measure how many frames it lets the loop skip before building it.
  5. Does the 3x to 4x crop upscale actually help RT-DETR, which was trained at 1920? Unmeasured.
  6. Do replays and close-ups need their own handling, since the ball there is large and the tracker has no pitch context?
  7. Where does the candidate pool live, and does it share the ball_candidates format so /ball_check can read it unchanged?
  8. Who owns the held-out registry, and how is time-span overlap between new matches checked?

Related: Architecture, Best pipeline and label needs, Tracking pipeline design, Ball tracking evaluation, TODO T-44 to T-49.

docs.title: Versioned datasets and progress tracking
docs.text: Status: datasets, ingest-all, eval results and CPU eval adapters are built (src/footy_track/datasets/, src/footy_track/feature_store/ingest_all.py, tests in tests/datasets/) and the /progress page is built (section 11). The nightly flow is planned, not built (section 12).

docs.title: 1. Goal
docs.text:
"A clear dataset for tracking, broadcast view, and pitch calibration that we can track dataset changes and performance changes."

Three independently versioned datasets, tracking, broadcast and calibration. Each has a train part and an eval part, taken from the one split authority (footy_track.splits.split_of). A version is bumped when the labels (or their split) change, and every model is scored on a dataset version, so two questions are always answerable:

  • what changed in the data? (the manifest diff between two versions)
  • what changed in performance? (eval_result, one row per dataset version x model x split x metric)

Why it is needed (found 2026-11-17): labelling never reached the feature store (every labeller writes JSON/JSONL, ingest was a manual CLI, no live store existed); a GT re-ingest replaces rows, so the store had no history; and the broadcast classifier's accuracy went from 0.98 to 0.41-0.44 when a Roboflow dataset changed underneath it with nothing recording that it had.

docs.title: 2. The pipeline
docs.text:
label files (labeller)                    DuckDB store                    snapshots                  results
ball_gt_marks/*.jsonl            \                                   datasets/tracking/vN/
ball_gt_marks/ball_checks/        \   ingest_all   feature_store.duckdb   datasets/broadcast/vN/    eval_result
calibration_gt/ frame_type/        >------------>  (detection, gt_frame,  datasets/calibration/vN/   (dataset version x
calibration_proposals/            /   idempotent    calibration, ...,                                  model x split/cohort)
broadcast_review/<video>.json    /    single writer  broadcast_label)  --datasets bump--> items.parquet + manifest.json
  1. python -m footy_track.feature_store.ingest_all copies every label source into the store.
  2. python -m footy_track.datasets bump all builds each dataset's item table from the store and writes a new immutable snapshot only if the content hash changed.
  3. Evaluations score a model on a snapshot and append rows to eval_result (python -m footy_track.datasets results ... or eval_adapters.evaluate_and_record).

The store is a rebuildable index over the label files; the snapshots are the record.

docs.title: 3. The three datasets and their items
docs.text:
An item is the unit that is counted, hashed, split and diffed. Every item has: item_id, split, match_key, clip (canonical clip id), game_id, frame_index, label_kind, tier, a canonical JSON payload, an item_hash and first_version.

dataset item (granularity) item_id label kinds payload tracking one labelled frame of a clip <game_id>:<frame> ball, other_boxes, no_ball, not_broadcast, check_only, empty every box (label, source, tier, rejected, x/y/w/h), the Ball Check verdicts on the frame, the sidecar's skip marker broadcast one human frame verdict <video stem>:<frame> yes, no, unsure verdict, plus the classifier's stored call (pred, p_yes), why it was sampled (reason), ts_s calibration one frame correspondence set <canonical clip>:<frame> homography, not_broadcast, too_few_points the human image to pitch point pairs, the fitted H (norm_image->pitch_m), distortion_k1, image size

Details that matter when reading the numbers:

  • tracking. The frame set is every frame a ball-GT sidecar mentions (gt_frame) plus every frame with a Ball Check verdict. ball = at least one ball box that no Ball Check rejected. no_ball and not_broadcast are the sidecar's own skip markers (the detection table drops them, so ingest keeps them in gt_frame). check_only = no sidecar box, only verdicts on detector candidates (hard negatives and positives from Ball Check). tier is the best tier among the frame's ball boxes (or all boxes when there is no ball): 1 human-placed (labeller), 2 machine box a human confirmed (human_checked, or a Ball Check ball/corrected verdict), 3 machine only. A consumer chooses its own GT rule (ball_eval uses tier 1, optionally tier 2); tier 3 is stored but is not ground truth. One physical clip can be several game_ids (arsenal_mancity_seg010 and arsenal_mancity_20250925_seg010): they stay separate items (each is a different sidecar) with the same canonical clip, so they always share a split.
  • broadcast. Today the only source is the broadcast review (labeller/broadcast_review.py): frames the classifier was unsure about plus a random sample, judged yes/no/unsure by a human. They have no clip, so a 6,000-frame window <match>_wNNNN stands in for one (splits.broadcast_window_id). unsure items are kept but never scored. The sampling is biased towards hard frames, so a stored classifier's accuracy over all frames is not its accuracy on a random frame; the headline is the random stratum only (see "Broadcast eval: random vs edge strata" in section 9).
  • calibration. Human GT only (calibration_gt/) plus the human frame_type/ flags. Machine proposals are stored in the store but are the thing being evaluated, not part of the dataset. A file is copied to every alias game_id of its clip; the dataset keeps one item per canonical clip and frame.

docs.title: 4. Split tiers
docs.text:
split comes from footy_track.splits.split_of(match_key, clip), never from a stored column (it would go stale as the registers grow). See data.md.

split meaning eval_heldout_match a whole match that is evaluation only (match_splits.json) eval_in_match one clip in five of a train match (clip_splits.json, sha1(clip) % 5 == 0) train everything else

Assignments are sticky and the eval set only grows. build raises if a needed register is missing (fail closed); FOOTY_CLIP_SPLITS_PREVIEW=1 lets build (read-only) show what the hash rule would give while clip_splits.json does not exist yet. bump refuses to write from missing registers unless --allow-preview (never do that for a version anyone will compare against).

docs.title: 5. Versioning rules
docs.text:
• A dataset's version is bumped only when its content hash changes; bump is idempotent and safe to run nightly.
  • Datasets version independently: new broadcast labels do not bump tracking.
  • Versions are integers starting at 1, parent = previous version. Snapshots are never edited or removed.
  • The content hash covers: item ids, splits, match, clip, game id, frame, label kind, tier and the label payload. It does not cover time stamps, paths, git sha, version numbers or first_version. A label edit, a new or removed item, or a split reassignment all change it.
  • Bump on a meaningful change (a labelling session, a new match, a new batch of Ball Check clips), not on every save; the nightly job does it for you.
  • A tag of the producing code (git_sha, git_dirty) is in the manifest but never in the hash.

docs.title: Content hash
docs.text: sha256 over a header line ({"dataset": ..., "schema": 1}) followed by one line per item sorted by item_id: [item_id, split, match_key, clip, game_id, frame_index, label_kind, tier, payload] as compact JSON. Payloads are canonical JSON: sorted keys, no spaces, floats rounded to 6 places. Loading a snapshot re-derives the hash and raises SnapshotTampered if it does not match the manifest (the next bump also refuses to build on a tampered parent). Changing ITEM_SCHEMA in datasets/items.py forces a new version.

docs.title: 6. Snapshot layout and immutability
docs.text:
Root: /mnt/storage/footy_data (env FOOTY_DATASETS_ROOT, then FOOTY_DATA; --root).

datasets/
  tracking/v1/items.parquet  manifest.json
  tracking/v2/...
  broadcast/v1/...
  calibration/v1/...

items.parquet columns: item_id, dataset, split, match_key, clip, game_id, frame_index, label_kind, tier, payload, item_hash, first_version. Snapshots are written to a temp directory, made read-only and renamed into place; an existing vN is never overwritten (SnapshotExists). Writes need the store's write lock. Every version is also indexed in the store's dataset_version table; the files are authoritative and bump re-syncs the table from them.

docs.title: 7. Manifest
docs.text:
manifest.json per version:

field meaning dataset, version, created_at, note identity content_hash, item_schema see section 5 parent_version, parent_content_hash null for v1 counts n_items; by_split; by_split_kind (split x label kind); by_split_tier; clips_by_split split_registers sha256 of match_splits.json and clip_splits.json, their paths, the in-match rule, preview (true if a register file was missing) n_items_unregistered_match items whose match is in neither register (they are treated as train-pool) git_sha, git_dirty code that built it diff_vs_parent items added / removed / changed in total and *_by_split; "changed" = same item id, different content

python -m footy_track.datasets diff <dataset> A B lists the added / removed / changed item ids.

docs.title: 8. Eval results
docs.text:
Table eval_result, append-only, in the feature store:

column meaning task tracking / broadcast / calibration dataset, dataset_version the snapshot the number was measured on split train, eval_heldout_match, eval_in_match, eval_all (both eval tiers) cohort_version NULL = the full current split; N = only items with first_version <= N model_name, model_version weights sha256, Roboflow version, or a proposals run id metric, value, n_items the number and how many items it covers run_at, code_sha when and with which code contaminated, contamination_note see section 10 (NULL = not checked)

Results are tied to the version they were measured on and are never joined to "current labels". A re-run appends; the view eval_result_latest is the newest run per (task, dataset, version, split, cohort, model, model_version, metric). record_results(...) / list_results(...) in footy_track.datasets.results; CLI: python -m footy_track.datasets results list|record.

docs.title: Cohorts: reading a growing eval set
docs.text:
Because the eval set only grows, eval(vN) contains eval(vN-1), and a model scored on v5 is not comparable to one scored on v2 on the full set. Each model run therefore records two lines per metric and eval split:

  • full current (cohort_version NULL): everything in the split at that version. Best estimate today.
  • fixed cohort (cohort_version = k): only items that were already in the dataset at version k. Apples to apples across every model scored on version >= k. Pick k = the version of the oldest model you still compare against.

evaluate_and_record(..., cohorts=[1]) writes both. A progress chart plots the cohort line for trend and the full line for the current truth.

docs.title: 9. Eval adapters
docs.text:
footy_track/datasets/eval_adapters.py: adapter.evaluate(model, dataset_version, split, cohort) -> EvalOutput(metrics, n_items); evaluate_and_record(...) runs one over every split and cohort, attaches contamination flags and records the rows.

adapter task status metrics model CalibrationAdapter calibration works, CPU success_at_5px, success_at_10px, mean_/median_reprojection_px, mean_reprojection_m, failed_rate, keypoint_agreement, coverage ProposalRunModel(run_id, gt_dirs): a stored proposals run in calibration_proposals/ (reuses prelabel.evaluate.eval_frame); any object with .proposal(item) works BroadcastAdapter broadcast works, CPU Headline (random stratum): accuracy, precision_yes, recall_yes, f1_yes, n_yes, n_no, n_random, plus accuracy_random, f1_yes_random. Diagnostic: accuracy_edge, f1_yes_edge, n_edge, accuracy_all_biased, f1_yes_all_biased, n_unknown StoredPredictionModel: the classifier's call recorded with each frame when it was queued for review (the number the review page shows). Any object with .says_yes(item) works BallTrackerAdapter tracking works on CPU given a candidate cache ball_precision_/recall_/wrong_per_prediction_ at 10 px and 25 px, clips_scored, clips_without_cache BallTrackerReplay(kind, cache_dir, ...): replays online/bidirectional/viterbi over <clip>.jsonl caches from ball_tracking_eval cache (reuses ball_eval.detection_replay) DetectorAdapter tracking works, CPU (scores stored GPU detections) per class player_/referee_: ap50, precision, recall, f1, f1_max; ball (ball_ = tier-1 human GT, ball_t12_ = human + confirmed): ap_iou50, ap_10px, ap_25px and precision / recall / F1 per rule; map50, coverage, *_n_gt DetectionStore(dir): <canonical clip>.npz per eval clip, written by datasets/detector_run.py

docs.title: Detector eval (tracking)
docs.text:
datasets/detector_run.py runs the detector once over every frame of every eval clip (GPU) and stores the raw detections (conf >= 0.1, all classes, dets/<clip>.npz) plus the ball candidates in the ball_tracking_eval cache format (cache/<clip>.jsonl); DetectorAdapter scores the stored detections on the CPU and BallTrackerAdapter replays trackers over the cache. Resumable per clip; a new dataset version only needs inference for clips with no detections yet.

  • Frame sourcing. An item is a labelled frame (game_id = video stem, frame_index into that video). Frames come from the clip video, decoded sequentially from frame 0 (frame-exact; seeking is not), from the video the labeller showed: labeller-registry clip dirs (the *_kf10 re-encodes) first, then <FOOTY_DATA>/clips. Videos and detections are keyed by canonical clip id (aliases are the same file).
  • Ground truth. Tier 1 (human) and tier 2 (machine box a human confirmed) boxes; rejected boxes are not GT; tier 3 boxes and coach / person / player_sub boxes are ignore regions (a detection on one is neither hit nor false positive). A frame is scored for a class only if it has GT of that class (ball: also no_ball frames; never not_broadcast), because labelling is not exhaustive: player / referee precision is a lower bound.
  • Matching. Players / referees: IoU >= 0.5. Ball: IoU >= 0.5 (reconciles with the leaderboard mAP50), and centre distance <= 10 px / 25 px (native px, the ball tracker's radii). The ball is ~11 px, so IoU 0.5 needs the centre within ~3 px and mostly measures box tightness; the 10 px rows say whether the ball was found, which is what tracking needs. P / R are at conf 0.3 (the pipeline default); AP is over all detections with 101-point interpolation (as Ultralytics, so a perfect detector scores 0.995).
  • Contamination. Flags come from detection_dataset/roboflow_dataset_11 (contamination_from_roboflow) when the rows are recorded on the mini; bournemouth_1st_seg070 (in-match eval) is in v11 train.

The Prefect side (jobs repo footy_nightly_datasets.py, footy-nightly-gpu) stages the weights / snapshot / videos to the desktop, runs this, pushes the cache to ball_tracking_cache/<sha12>/ on the mini and hands the rows to the mini (gpu_eval_results/pending/ then record-rows; the desktop never opens the store).

docs.title: Broadcast eval: random vs edge strata
docs.text:
Broadcast review frames are not a random sample. broadcast_select.select picks the frames nearest the decision boundary (edge_mid, edge_boundary; legacy value edge) plus a few random ones, and the item payload carries that reason. In broadcast v1 (72 in-match eval items from one match) 49 items (68%) are edge frames with stored p_yes about 0.48-0.52, and only 23 are random. On edge frames any preprocessing difference flips the call, so accuracy there is noise:

frames stored calls JPEG re-score video-seek re-score edge (49) 0.33 0.76 0.59 random (23) 0.87 0.87 0.87 all 72 (edge-weighted) 0.50 0.79

There is no join, threshold or weights bug; the 0.50 vs 0.79 gap is the edge weighting. So:

  • BroadcastAdapter headline metrics (accuracy, f1_yes, precision_yes, recall_yes, n_yes, n_no) are computed on the random stratum only, with n_random. accuracy_random / f1_yes_random repeat them under the explicit stratum name.
  • accuracy_edge, f1_yes_edge, n_edge and the all-frames accuracy_all_biased, f1_yes_all_biased are diagnostic only.
  • Legacy items with no reason (or any value other than random / edge*) are never assumed random: nothing records that they were sampled at random. They count in n_unknown and *_all_biased only, and are excluded from the headline and the edge stratum. (Only a reason of random in the review file says so.)
  • /progress shows the headline with its n, greys the diagnostic metrics (tooltip says why), and warns "small eval sample" when the headline n is below 50. A result recorded before this split (no n_random) is flagged "all frames, edge-weighted".
  • Reviews of held-out matches should use the eval-oriented selection of broadcast_select (mostly random, few edge), since held-out labels are never used for training.

docs.title: 10. Contamination flags
docs.text:
A number is only an honest estimate if the model did not train on the items it is scored on. contamination_flags(TrainingData, dataset_version) returns a flag per result split:

  • Roboflow / YOLO export dir (TrainingData(roboflow_dir=...)): splits.contamination maps each training image name to a match / clip and counts those that belong to a held-out match or an eval clip. Images that name a match but not a clip (frames of a full-match video) cannot be placed, and the note says so, so "not contaminated" can still hide in-match overlap for those models.
  • A dataset version (TrainingData(dataset=, version=)): eval items that share a clip (in-match) or a match (held-out) with that version's train items. Sticky assignment makes this empty unless a register was edited.
  • Not declared: every flag is NULL (unchecked), never an implicit "clean".

contaminated is true / false / NULL; the note says how many and which clips. results record --train-roboflow-dir DIR or --train-dataset D --train-version N sets it on the CLI. Known cases on 2026-11-17 (preview split): the Roboflow v11 detector has 212 of 1,035 train images in an eval clip (bournemouth_1st_seg070); the broadcast classifier's Roboflow 9 / 10 train sets hold about 13% Nottingham Forest (held-out) frames. Such results should be recorded with contaminated = true until the models are retrained on authority-based exports.

docs.title: 11. /progress page (built)
docs.text:
http://<labeller>:8011/progress (linked from the hub), JSON at /api/progress (labeller/progress.py, progress_routes.py, web/progress.html). It is the one view of project progress and is global: the ?dataset= labelling-dataset parameter is ignored.

Main view: three sections (Tracking, Broadcast view, Pitch calibration), two small line charts each. X is the dataset version (v1, v2, ...; the date is in the hover tooltip; one version draws dots, not a stretched axis). Hover or tap a version for a tooltip.

  1. Dataset size: items per version for train, eval (in-match) and eval (held-out match), from the snapshot manifests only (never items.parquet); Y starts at 0.
  2. Performance: one headline metric per model, at most about 3 lines, Y 0 to 1. Which metrics: the PERFORMANCE_SERIES dict at the top of labeller/progress.py (metric key, split, model_name pattern, how to pick one run when several model_versions share a dataset version). Today: tracking = ball F1 @10px on the held-out split, player recall on in-match eval, ball-tracker recall @10px on held-out; broadcast = accuracy (random stratum only) of the re-scored classifier and of the calls made at review time, in-match eval; calibration = success_at_5px, in-match eval. Always the full current eval (cohort_version NULL). Tooltip: value, n_items, model name @ version. A dashed segment means the model changed between the two versions. A contaminated result (contaminated = true) is a hollow marker, explained by one footnote under the charts.

Everything else is still on the page, collapsed under one Details section (open it, or load /progress?details=1):

  1. Dataset versions table (created_at, items by split, label kinds, diff vs the parent) and model performance: per model and metric, the value at each dataset version as a line chart plus two tables, "full current eval" and "fixed cohort". A contaminated result is drawn red with a warning mark; unknown contamination (NULL) is amber with a "?"; neither is ever styled as clean. The broadcast edge and all-biased metrics are greyed as diagnostic, and the headline carries its random-frame n with a small-sample warning.
  2. Split health. Matches held-out vs train (match_splits.json) and clips eval vs train (clip_splits.json), the latest version's eval counts per dataset, and warnings: zero held-out eval items (a call to action; broadcast has none until a held-out match's broadcast-review frames are labelled), no in-match eval, items in an unregistered match, a preview split, and split registers that changed since the latest snapshot (run bump).
  3. Empty states with the exact command: no store (python -m footy_track.feature_store.ingest_all), no versions (python -m footy_track.datasets bump all), no results (a results record example), no clip register (python -m footy_track.splits assign --apply). Missing, unreadable or locked files degrade the affected section; the page never returns a 500. On the main view a chart with no data just says "no results yet".

The JSON keeps every field the Details view needs and adds datasets.<ds>.charts ({versions, size, performance}), which is what the two charts draw.

Implementation: the store is opened read_only for a single query under the shared store lock and closed again (a writer mid-ingest gives a "store busy" note, not a hang). The payload is cached for 60 s and invalidated early when a manifest, the store (or its WAL) or a register changes; ?refresh=true forces a rebuild. Charts are inline SVG, no external scripts.

docs.title: 12. Planned, not built yet
docs.text:
• Nightly Prefect flow: ingest_all, then bump all, then queue evals for any new version (GPU on the desktop, the rest on the mini). Its job is to make the CLI above run unattended.
  • Not wired yet: detector P / R / mAP50; more broadcast sources than the review (e.g. the frame_type not-broadcast flags); Roboflow imports into tracking; a per-clip eval_result for paired bootstrap.

docs.title: 13. How to
docs.text:
# 1. ingest every label source (idempotent; --dry-run parses into memory only)
python -m footy_track.feature_store.ingest_all                # store: $FOOTY_FEATURE_STORE or /mnt/storage/footy_data/feature_store/feature_store.duckdb

# 2. what would change?  (read-only)
python -m footy_track.datasets build tracking
# 3. write the next version if (and only if) the content changed
python -m footy_track.datasets bump all --note "after Nottingham Forest ball checks"
python -m footy_track.datasets list
python -m footy_track.datasets show tracking v2
python -m footy_track.datasets diff tracking v1 v2

# 4. record a result (contamination from the model's training export)
python -m footy_track.datasets results record --task broadcast --dataset broadcast --dataset-version 2 \
    --split eval_heldout_match --model broadcast_classifier --model-version <sha256> \
    --metric accuracy --value 0.91 --n-items 120 --train-roboflow-dir /path/to/roboflow_dataset_10
python -m footy_track.datasets results list --dataset broadcast

In Python: from footy_track.datasets import eval_adapters as ea; ea.evaluate_and_record(ea.BroadcastAdapter(), ea.StoredPredictionModel(), load_version("broadcast"), db, cohorts=[1]).

Ingest takes an exclusive lock on <store>.lock (single writer; a second writer fails fast with StoreLocked). bump and results record take it too; build and results list take the shared lock. Only the broadcast_label, gt_frame and the eval / version tables are new; the other tables are the existing ones (feature_store.md).

Environment on the Mac mini: duckdb 1.3.x to 1.5.3 only (2.0 crashes without AVX2); keep CPU use light (one heavy process at a time). A full ingest of the real labels takes a couple of minutes.

Ingest notes: GT sidecars and calibration files are read from every marks_dir of the labeller's labeller_datasets.json (the calib set, the held-out Nottingham Forest sets, the broadcast-review set), so backup copies (ball_gt_marks.bak-*, ball_gt_marks_MERGED) are never read. Ball Check logs of one clip in several dirs are merged by timestamp. Deleting a file is not propagated (the labeller truncates, it does not delete); emptying a file is.

docs.title: 14. Why not LanceDB
docs.text:
A LanceDB feature store was designed and spiked first (a native table version per write, tags, time travel, merge_insert upserts). It was rejected because import lancedb / import lance abort with SIGILL on the Mac mini (i7-2635QM: AVX, no AVX2), and the mini hosts Prefect, the labeller and /mnt/storage. Tested and all crash: lancedb 0.15.0, 0.22.0, 0.30.0, 0.41.0 and pylance 0.19.1. The same install works on desktop-ubuntu (Ryzen 5 5600G). DuckDB 1.3 to 1.5.3 works on the mini (2.0 does not).

DuckDB plus content-hashed Parquet snapshots delivers the three goals that matter (independent versions, tracked results, a growing eval set) on the hardware that exists. Revisit if the host changes (a CPU with AVX2, or the store moving to the desktop): Lance would add native time travel and cheaper incremental versions, nothing else we need.

docs.title: Appendix: Lance facts worth keeping (from the rejected design)
docs.text:
Measured with lancedb 0.41.0 / duckdb 1.5.3 on desktop-ubuntu, for whoever revisits it:

  • Every write is a new table version; checkout, restore and per-table tags exist, but tags are per table, so a multi-table dataset version = the same tag on each table plus a manifest row.
  • optimize(cleanup_older_than=...) prunes untagged versions and keeps tagged ones; never run it while a reader or writer is active.
  • merge_insert is the upsert. A no-op merge still creates a version; unconditional when_matched_update_all rewrites unchanged rows; four concurrent threads inserting the same new key produced four duplicate rows (there is no primary key), so every writer needs a file lock plus a row_hash pre-diff to avoid no-op versions.
  • Commit atomicity relies on object-store put-if-not-exists; the spec says nothing about local disk or NFS, so multi-host writers over NFS are untested.
  • The DuckDB lance extension returned 404 for duckdb 1.5.3; the working route is con.register(name, table.to_arrow()).
  • The design's useful ideas live on here: the dataset manifest, the eval_result schema with cohorts, a broadcast_label table, first_version, and the consumer map below.

Consumer / producer map (writers all go through FeatureStore; readers of JSON sidecars are unaffected): ingest_gt (per-clip delete then upsert), ingest_calibration, ball_checks (per-row UPDATE reviewed, the riskiest to port), importers, ingest/detect_objects, difficulty (uses the private _conn), export_training_dataset (reads via query; its per-row UPDATE dataset_tag is replaced by recording an export as a dataset version), claude_verify_v2 (JSONL only). ball_eval, labeller/* and broadcast_review read sidecars directly.

docs.title: Feature Store — Design
docs.text:
Status: IMPLEMENTED (v1) · Code: src/footy_track/feature_store/ · Tests: tests/feature_store/

Dataset versions, the one-shot ingest_all, and model results (eval_result, dataset_version, broadcast_label, gt_frame tables) are in datasets_and_progress.md.

This document proposes a single, queryable feature store for footy-track: the consolidated home for everything we know about a match's frames — per-frame metadata, broadcast classification, pitch segmentation, object detections from multiple sources, and (later) tracks and pitch projections.

It supersedes and consolidates the scattered per-stage Parquet artifacts sketched in ../pipelines.md §Data model (frames.parquet, detections.parquet, geometry.parquet, ocr_clock.parquet, embeddings.parquet) and folds in the canonical track store from player_tracking_format.md. See §9 for how the migration relates to those documents.

It honours the cross-stage invariants in ../system_design.md §4 — ContinuousTime as the only canonical timestamp, normalised top-left xywh boxes, class labels from constants.py, and monotone non-reused track IDs.

docs.title: 1. Goals and non-goals
docs.text:
Goals

  • One portable store per environment that a human or a downstream consumer (footy-stats, FiftyOne, evaluation, overlays) can query with a single SELECT and no bespoke join glue.
  • Hold, for every frame of every game: identity (path, resolution, frame index), time (ContinuousTime + GameTime + half), and the outputs of every analysis stage — broadcast classification, pitch segmentation, calibration, and object detections.
  • Support multiple independent detection sources over the same frames (hand-labelled ground truth, SAM 3, YOLO runs, future trackers) coexisting without overwriting each other, each carrying its own confidence and model version.
  • Be idempotent: re-ingesting the same run must not duplicate rows (footy-stats invariant).
  • Allow schema evolution — adding a new stage's columns or a new source must not require rewriting existing data.

Non-goals

  • A query API or serving layer — that is footy-stats' job. This store is the substrate footy-stats (and notebooks) read from.
  • Re-identification, team assignment, jersey OCR, event extraction — these populate columns reserved here but are designed elsewhere.
  • The tracker/detector algorithms themselves.
  • Real-time/streaming ingestion — this design is batch-on-completion. §10 notes the streaming extension point.

docs.title: 2. The core decision: one store, not one table
docs.text:
The request is "a single Parquet/DuckDB table with lots of data in it." The honest engineering answer is: a single DuckDB database file (the store) containing a small set of normalised tables at their natural grains, plus a wide frame_features view that presents the per-frame world as one table.

A literally-single physical table fails on grain:

Fact Natural grain Rows for a 90-min game @ 25fps frame metadata, clock, broadcast flag, pitch polygon, homography 1 row per frame ~135 k object detections (per source, per run) N rows per frame (≈25 objects × M sources) millions game metadata (teams, venue, time mapping) 1 row per game tens processing provenance (model, params, run time) 1 row per run hundreds

Forcing detections into the frame row means array-of-struct columns that are awkward to filter and explode; forcing frame metadata onto every detection row means massive duplication and update anomalies (change one pitch polygon → rewrite 25 M rows). So we normalise by grain and denormalise on read via views. The user gets "one table" ergonomics (SELECT * FROM frame_features); the storage stays sane.

docs.title: Why DuckDB as the store, Parquet as the substrate
docs.text:
• DuckDB file = the single store. One feature_store.duckdb is the portable, single-file artifact the request asks for. It gives real tables, constraints, UPSERT (idempotency), and SQL across grains.
  • Parquet = the on-disk table format and interchange. Each table is also materialisable as a partitioned Parquet dataset (store/<table>/game_id=<id>/part.parquet) for DVC versioning, for consumers that don't want DuckDB, and so DuckDB can query it in place (read_parquet) without import.
  • DuckDB reads/writes Parquet natively, so the two are the same data in two skins. We treat Parquet as the source of truth on disk and the DuckDB file as a fast, constraint-enforcing index over it (rebuildable from Parquet at any time). This keeps the store DVC-friendly and reproducible.

Status check, 2026-11-08

The design above is not what runs. DuckDB is the only store anyone writes to. A Parquet export exists (store.py:270-326) but no workflow uses it, so DuckDB is the source of truth. And game_id is a clip stem for GT imports (for example astonvilla_seg080), not a match as section 3.1 suggests. See section 7.1.

docs.title: 3. Schema overview
docs.text:
Seven tables plus five convenience views. All timestamps ContinuousTime (seconds, float64) per ../timings.md. All boxes normalised top-left xywh in [0,1].

game ──1:N── frame ──1:N── detection
  │             │              │
  │             │              └── source/run carried per row (see §6)
  │             ├── pitch_segmentation: inlined on frame (§5.3)
  │             └── calibration ──1:N── pitch_keypoint (source/run per row, §3.7)
  └── run (provenance for every produced artifact, §7)

track / track_meta: derived from detection, see §8

docs.title: 3.1 game — one row per match
docs.text:
Column Type Notes game_id VARCHAR PK despite the name, usually a clip stem: ingest_gt uses the GT sidecar stem (mancity_seg010), detect_objects the frames folder name, Roboflow imports a match-level stem (arsenal_mancity_20250925). Not canonical; see §3.1a home_team VARCHAR away_team VARCHAR match_date DATE nullable venue VARCHAR nullable source_video_uri VARCHAR original video path/URI fps DOUBLE nominal sampling/extraction fps width INTEGER native video resolution height INTEGER half1_start_continuous_s DOUBLE always 0.0 (kept explicit) half2_start_continuous_s DOUBLE GameTime→ContinuousTime offset for 2nd half (GameMetadata, ../timings.md) game_start_wallclock TIMESTAMP nullable schema_version VARCHAR store schema version this row was written under

This subsumes the GameMetadata block previously living in tracks_meta.json.

docs.title: 3.1a Clip identity (canonical clip id)
docs.text:
One physical clip has several names across the data plane, and game_id inherits whichever one the importer saw. footy_track.clip_id.canonical_clip_id maps them to one id, <match>_<kind><NNN> (date infix dropped, number zero-padded to 3):

Names on disk (same video, verified via the ballcheck_clips/ and eval_data/clips/ symlinks) Canonical id arsenal_mancity_20250925_segNNN (clips, machine labels, candidates), arsenal_mancity_segNNN, mancity_segNNN arsenal_mancity_segNNN arsenal_mancity_20250925_partNNN (split_video_10s, a different cut from segNNN), mancity_partNNN arsenal_mancity_partNNN Arsenal - Aston Villa_segNNN, astonvilla_segNNN arsenal_astonvilla_segNNN Bournemouth vs Arsenal 1_segNNN, bournemouth_1st_segNNN, bournemouth_broadcast_segNNN, bournemouth_segNNN arsenal_bournemouth_1st_segNNN arsenal_mancity_example_video, arsenal_example arsenal_example

Anything else passes through unchanged (minus extension). Where it is used:

  • Training export: eval exclusion compares canonical ids, so an eval clip stored under another alias is excluded; the by-clip split assigns whole alias groups (keyed by their smallest game_id, so an alias-free store splits as before). The manifest lists the groups under clip_aliases.
  • ball_check save_box: a correction on a raw-named candidate goes into the clip's existing GT sidecar (labeller README LAB-1013a).
  • ball_eval: EvalClip.clip_id; EvalDataset.from_dirs(..., resolve_aliases=True) matches GT to a video under another alias (off by default, as it changes which GT files are scored).
  • ingest_gt: deliberately not canonicalised. game_id stays the sidecar stem: that file is the unit ingest (re)imports and the gt_import:<game_id> run group, and two aliases' sidecars would otherwise collide on the detection PK.

Find aliases with aliases_of(name, names) / group_by_clip(names), or the read-only report python -m footy_track.clip_id --db <store> [dirs...].

Migration note. Existing stores keep their alias game_ids and need no change for the export to be leak-free. To canonicalise a store anyway, run the report to list the game_ids that would collapse, merge those sidecars by hand (they hold separately labelled frames), and re-ingest into a fresh store. Never UPDATE game_id in place.

docs.title: 3.2 frame — one row per (game, frame)
docs.text:
The per-frame spine. One row whether or not the frame is a usable broadcast view (non-broadcast frames are recorded, not dropped — invariant #5).

Column Type Notes game_id VARCHAR FK → game frame_index INTEGER zero-based frame number within the game frame_uri VARCHAR path to the extracted image (full_video_frames/*.jpg) width INTEGER frame resolution (may differ from game native if downscaled) height INTEGER continuous_time_s DOUBLE canonical time, seconds from kickoff half TINYINT 1 or 2; nullable until time-mapped game_time_s DOUBLE referee/broadcast clock seconds in-half; nullable broadcast classification is_broadcast BOOLEAN from §2.2 classifier; nullable until run broadcast_confidence FLOAT nullable broadcast_model_version VARCHAR FK → run.run_id or a model tag pitch segmentation (§5.3) pitch_polygon LIST<STRUCT(x DOUBLE, y DOUBLE)> final pitch boundary, normalised; nullable pitch_seg_threshold FLOAT the allowance/threshold used to derive the polygon pitch_seg_confidence FLOAT nullable pitch_seg_model_version VARCHAR FK → run.run_id calibration (§5.4) homography LIST<DOUBLE> (len 9) DEPRECATED — see §3.7; flattened 3×3 H; nullable calibration_quality FLOAT DEPRECATED — see §3.7; nullable calibration_model_version VARCHAR DEPRECATED — see §3.7

PK: (game_id, frame_index). The clock fields come from the OCR stage (ocr_clock.parquet is absorbed here); time-mapping fills half / continuous_time_s via game.half2_start_continuous_s.

Design note — pitch segmentation is inlined on frame; calibration is not (any more). Segmentation is strictly per-frame and read alongside the frame, so it stays inlined with one "final" polygon per frame; if we ever need to compare multiple segmentation runs it graduates to a source-tagged table (§11). Calibration already has that need (human GT, Claude proposals, classical runs over the same frames), so it graduated: see §3.7. The three inline homography / calibration_quality / calibration_model_version columns are deprecated (kept so old DBs and FrameRow stay valid; nothing writes or reads them, none of the views use them). Use frame_calibration_best.

docs.title: 3.3 detection — one row per (game, frame, source, object)
docs.text:
The high-volume table. Every detected object from every source/run is a row.

Column Type Notes game_id VARCHAR FK → game frame_index INTEGER FK → frame continuous_time_s DOUBLE denormalised from frame for time-range scans without a join detection_id BIGINT per-frame object index (0..N-1) within (game_id, source, run_id, frame_index); see §6 source VARCHAR (dict) hand_label | yolo | sam3 | bytetrack | … (§6) run_id VARCHAR FK → run; pins model + params + version label VARCHAR (dict) class from constants.py confidence FLOAT [0,1]; 1.0 (or null) for hand labels bbox_x FLOAT normalised top-left x bbox_y FLOAT bbox_w FLOAT bbox_h FLOAT mask_ref VARCHAR nullable; pointer to RLE/PNG mask sidecar for SAM3 (§5.5) track_id INTEGER nullable; set by the tracking stage (§8) is_interpolated BOOLEAN tracker fill vs raw detection (§8)

PK: (game_id, source, run_id, frame_index, detection_id). detection_id is the per-frame object index, so detectors emit 0..N-1 per frame with no need for a run-global counter; re-ingesting one frame's detections upserts cleanly (GT-sidecar ingest additionally deletes the clip's gt_import_* rows first, see §7). Partitioned on disk by game_id then source (§6) so a single source's detections are a cheap column/partition scan and one source can be rewritten without touching others.

docs.title: 3.4 track_meta — one row per track (§8)
docs.text:
Per-track summary (label, span, identity). Kept separate from detection because it is updated post-hoc (re-ID, team, jersey) without rewriting the row store. Replaces the tracks block of tracks_meta.json.

Column Type Notes game_id VARCHAR source VARCHAR the tracker source (e.g. bytetrack) run_id VARCHAR FK → run track_id INTEGER monotone within (game_id, source, run_id), never reused label VARCHAR representative class start_frame / end_frame INTEGER inclusive start_continuous_time_s / end_continuous_time_s DOUBLE last real detection team_id VARCHAR nullable — TODO, team assignment jersey_number INTEGER nullable — TODO, OCR player_id VARCHAR nullable — TODO, identity reid_parent_track_id INTEGER nullable — re-ID link (invariant #6)

docs.title: 3.5 run — one row per processing run (provenance)
docs.text:
Every produced value (a broadcast flag, a polygon, a detection set) names the run_id that produced it. This is how we get reproducibility and how two YOLO runs with different weights coexist (§6).

Column Type Notes run_id VARCHAR PK stable id, e.g. yolo11n_v3__2026-06-10 or a content hash stage VARCHAR broadcast | detection | pitch_seg | calibration | tracking source VARCHAR the source value rows from this run carry model_name VARCHAR e.g. yolo11n.pt, sam3.pt, human model_version VARCHAR weights tag / git sha / roboflow dataset version params_json VARCHAR JSON of thresholds/config (e.g. conf threshold, tracker yaml) created_at TIMESTAMP when the run was produced code_version VARCHAR footy-track git sha schema_version VARCHAR store schema version

docs.title: 3.6 Views (the "one table" ergonomics)
docs.text:
• frame_features — frame ⨝ game: every per-frame fact plus game metadata, one row per frame. The "single wide table" the request describes.
  • detections_enriched — detection ⨝ frame ⨝ run: each detection with its frame's time/broadcast context and its run's model metadata.
  • tracks_enriched — detection ⨝ track_meta: tracked detections with per-track identity.
  • frame_calibration_best — one calibration per (game, frame) chosen from the calibration table by the precedence in §3.7.
  • detections_on_pitch — detection ⨝ frame_calibration_best, projected to pitch metres in SQL (§3.7).

Views cost nothing on disk and can be CREATE TABLE AS materialised if a consumer wants a frozen flat export.

docs.title: 3.7 calibration, pitch_keypoint and the calibration views
docs.text:
calibration — one row per (game_id, source, run_id, frame_index) (source-tagged like detection, so human GT, Claude proposals and classical runs coexist):

Column Type Notes game_id, source, run_id, frame_index PK. source ∈ hand_label | claude | classical | (future) model; run_id FK → run (stage calibration, params_json = model / prompt_version / effort …) H DOUBLE[9] row-major 3×3, normalised image → pitch metres (origin centre spot, +x long axis), exactly what PitchProjector applies. NULL only for failed rows h_convention VARCHAR normalised_image_to_pitch_m (the only one the views understand; the importer rejects others) quality DOUBLE [0,1] projector gate. Machine rows: the proposal score. Human rows: 1.0 mean_err_px, mean_err_m, n_points, n_inliers fit diagnostics (mean_err_px = mean of per-point err_px) pitch_length, pitch_width, image_width, image_height dims the H was solved for method VARCHAR dlt | ransac | … review_status VARCHAR hand | proposed | accepted | rejected | failed reviewed BOOLEAN a human looked (true for GT, accepted, rejected) origin_source, origin_run_id, origin_status for GT rows that began as an accepted/edited proposal: which proposal (origin_status ∈ accepted/edited) failure VARCHAR reason when failed view_end, camera_side VARCHAR machine view hints (L/R end, camera side) created_at TIMESTAMP record time (UTC) dataset_tag VARCHAR importer that wrote the row (calibration_gt | calibration_proposals); scopes replace-on-reimport

pitch_keypoint — one row per correspondence behind a calibration row, PK (game_id, source, run_id, frame_index, point_idx): keypoint_id (nullable — free clicks have none), u, v (normalised image), pitch_x, pitch_y (metres), is_inlier, err_px, dataset_tag.

Both are Parquet-partitioned by game_id, source like detection.

frame_calibration_best — one row per (game_id, frame_index), carrying the winner's source, run_id and tier. Precedence:
